items.readable_text:
Content:
When the number of observations [MATH: n] of a binomial random variable is large, it can be difficult to calculate binomial probabilities due to the extremely large numbers involved. However, provided that some constraints are satisfied, we can closely approximate a binomial distribution as a Poisson distribution.

Content:
For example, suppose that at a lightbulb factory, [MATH: 0.5\%] of lightbulbs are defective. If a company manufactures [MATH: 1\,000] lightbulbs, what is the probability that [MATH: 10] of them will be defective?

Content:
Let [MATH: X] be the number of defective lightbulbs. If there are [MATH: n=1\,000] lightbulbs and the probability of any single lightbulb being defective is [MATH: p=0.5\% = 0.005,] then we can calculate [MATH: P(X=10)] using the probability mass function for the binomial distribution, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P(X = 10) = ((1000)/(10))(0.005)^{10}(0.995)^{990}]

Content:
However, this product is difficult to compute because

Content:
- the binomial coefficient is huge:
[MATH: \binom{1\,000}{10} = \dfrac{1\,000!}{990! \cdot 10!} = 263\,409\,560\,461\,970\,212\,832\,400]
- the power [MATH: (0.005)^{10}] is extremely small:
[MATH: (0.005)^{10} = 0.000\,000\,000\,000\,000\,000\,000\,009\,765\,625]

Content:
Thankfully, it turns out that when [MATH: n] is large, and [MATH: p] is small, we can approximate a binomial distribution using a Poisson distribution with rate [MATH: \lambda = np.] In our case, we have
[MATH: \lambda = np = (1\,000)(0.005) = 5.]

Content:
Using the Poisson approximation, the calculation becomes much more tractable. We get

Content:
[MATH: P(X = 10)|≈ (5^{10}e^{− 5})/(10!); ≈ (9765625e^{− 5})/(3628800); ≈ 0.018133]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 6] decimal places.

Content:
This is indeed very close to the binomial probability, which is

Content:
[MATH: P(X = 10)|= ((1000)/(10))(0.005)^{10}(0.995)^{990}; ≈ 0.017996]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 6] decimal places.

Content:
Note: There's not a single broadly accepted rule of thumb for using the Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution. Here, we will use the rule of thumb to use the Poisson approximation when [MATH: n>20] and [MATH: p<0.05.]

A rule of thumb is that we can approximate a binomial random variable using the Poisson distribution when [MATH: n>20] and [MATH: p< 0.05.]

    • [MATH: n] is not large enough: [MATH: n=10 \ngtr 20 \quad \color{red}\times]

  • Probability II can be approximated using the Poisson distribution.

    • [MATH: n] is large enough: [MATH: n=50 > 20 \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

    • [MATH: p] is small enough: [MATH: p = 2\% = 0.02 < 0.05 \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

  • Probability III cannot be approximated using the Poisson distribution.

    • [MATH: n] is large enough: [MATH: n=40 > 20 \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

    • [MATH: p] is not small enough: [MATH: p = 6\% = 0.06 \nless 0.05 \quad \color{red}\times]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

sections.normalized_html: The probability that an expert typist mistypes a single letter is [MATH: 0.003.] Using the Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that the typist will mistype at most [MATH: 4] letters on a page containing [MATH: 2\,000] letters.
sections.readable_text: The probability that an expert typist mistypes a single letter is [MATH: 0.003.] Using the Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that the typist will mistype at most [MATH: 4] letters on a page containing [MATH: 2\,000] letters.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of mistyped letters on the page. Then, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(2\,000, 0.003).]

As a general rule of thumb, we can approximate a binomial random variable using the Poisson distribution when [MATH: n > 20] and [MATH: p < 0.05.]

There are [MATH: n=2\,000>20] letters and the probability that an individual letter is mistyped is [MATH: p = 0.003 < 0.05,] so we can use a Poisson approximation.

The Poisson approximation will use the rate

[MATH: \lambda = np = (2\,000)(0.003) = 6.]

Substituting [MATH: \lambda = 6] into the Poisson probability mass function, we get

[MATH: f(x)|= (λ^{x}e^{− λ})/(x!); = (6^{x}e^{− 6})/(x!).]

The probability of having [MATH: 4] or fewer mistyped letters is

[MATH: P(X ≤ 4)|= P(0) + P(1) + P(2) + P(3) + P(4); ≈ f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3) + f(4); ≈ (6^{0}e^{− 6})/(0!) + (6^{1}e^{− 6})/(1!) + (6^{2}e^{− 6})/(2!) + (6^{3}e^{− 6})/(3!) + (6^{4}e^{− 6})/(4!); ≈ 0.285,]

rounded to three decimal places.
